script:
Think about opening a shared document. Your device sends a request through networks to the systems providing that service. Computing equipment handles the request, storage holds the information, and a response travels back.

The animation follows that sequence. The physical systems underneath stay necessary throughout: electricity powers the equipment, and cooling removes the heat it produces. A simple action on your device can depend on many connected systems, even though the service hides most of that complexity.

script:
In a conventional example, the normal supply passes through distribution and an uninterruptible power supply, or U P S, before reaching equipment. If the incoming source fails, stored energy can bridge the transition while a backup generator starts.

The animation illustrates that sequence. Actual designs differ, and backup operation depends on capacity, fuel, controls and maintenance. A generator alone doesn't mean there can be no interruption at the equipment.

script:
When exhaust mixes back into the intake stream, cooling capacity can be wasted and some equipment can receive warmer air than intended. The animation follows supply air through equipment and shows a separate return path.

Containment supports that separation. It still needs appropriate airflow, cooling capacity and controls. A barrier by itself doesn't prove that every equipment inlet receives the conditions it needs.

script:
Adding equipment changes more than the number of empty rack positions. It can increase electrical demand, heat-removal requirements and network traffic at different rates.

In this illustrative animation, the cooling allocation reaches its limit while mounting space remains available. The values explain a relationship, not a recommended rack design. The practical lesson is to identify the limiting budget before deciding that another device can be installed.

script:
Virtualization lets software present and manage logical computing environments on physical resources. In a virtual-machine example, a hypervisor manages the guest systems and their access to the host hardware.

Containers provide another arrangement: they share the kernel of their host operating environment. The animation traces a virtual machine’s physical dependency. More activity in an application can create more demand on processors, memory, storage and networks, with consequences for electricity and heat. Abstraction makes resources easier to use and manage; it doesn't remove their physical limits.
